summary: This informational RFC describes an EDNS0 option, in active use, that carries information about the network that originated a DNS query and the network the response can be cached for. It has known operational and privacy shortcomings, so a revision was expected.

plainLanguage.summary: EDNS Client Subnet lets a recursive DNS resolver pass part of the client's network address to an authoritative server. The server can tailor its answer and state which network range the answer fits, but the address information creates privacy and caching costs.

does edns client subnet leak my ip address
subtitle: How DNS resolvers can share a limited part of a client's network address with authoritative servers.

tldr.problem: An authoritative DNS server may tailor an answer based on the client's network, but a recursive resolver normally exposes only its own address.
tldr.mechanism: The EDNS Client Subnet option sends a truncated client address and prefix length; the response states the network scope for which the answer can be cached.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents an option already in use and describes privacy, cache, and security limitations. It recommends that nameserver software leave the feature off by default.

today: RFC 7871 is an Informational document published in May 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its abstract describes ECS as in active use and says a revision would be worked through the IETF, but the text does not report whether that happened.

sections.title: Why DNS Carries Client Network Information
sections.content:
Some authoritative nameservers return different answers based on the network location of the person asking. A recursive resolver normally makes the query itself, so the authoritative server sees the resolver's address rather than the client's. This can produce a less suitable answer when the resolver serves clients in different network locations.

RFC 7871 defines the EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) option so an intermediate resolver can provide a limited amount of client network information. The authoritative server may use that information to tailor its answer and indicate the address range for which the answer is intended. ECS is optional and the RFC recommends that nameserver software disable it by default.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS server usually sees the resolver's address, not the client's network. ECS lets a resolver share a limited part of the client address so the server can choose a more suitable answer.

sections.title: The ECS Option Fields
sections.content:
The ECS option uses code 8 and includes an address family, a source prefix length, a scope prefix length, and address bits. Family 1 means IPv4 and family 2 means IPv6. The source prefix length says how many leftmost address bits are sent; the remaining bits are omitted and the last transmitted octet is padded with zero bits.

The scope prefix length says how many address bits define the network covered by the response. Queries must set the scope length to zero. A responding authoritative server echoes the family, source length, and address from the query, then supplies the scope length for its answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The option identifies IPv4 or IPv6 and says how many leading address bits are included. The response adds a scope length to show which network range can use the answer.

sections.title: Sending ECS and Responding
sections.content:
Recursive resolvers generally add ECS when querying an authoritative nameserver. They choose a source prefix length no longer than the incoming query allows and should send fewer bits than the full address for privacy. A stub resolver can request that no client address bits be sent by using a source prefix length of zero.

An authoritative server that supports ECS includes the option in its reply when the query contained ECS, even if the address did not affect its answer. A server that does not support ECS should ignore the option and must not echo it merely to signal lack of support. A scope longer than the source prefix means the server needed a more specific address; a shorter scope means the answer applies more broadly.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver can limit the address detail it sends, and a stub can ask it to send none. The server's scope value tells the resolver how broadly it can reuse the answer.

sections.title: Caching Network-Specific Answers
sections.content:
An ECS-aware resolver stores answer records with the network scope indicated by the response. When it receives a later query, it matches the requested name, type, and class, then selects an applicable network entry using the longest matching prefix. If no suitable network entry exists, it resolves the name as usual rather than returning a tailored answer to the wrong client.

Network-specific caching can increase cache size, reduce cache hits, and increase server load. The RFC also notes interoperability ambiguities around negative answers and says Authority and Additional records must not be tied to an ECS network scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver labels a cached answer with the network range it covers. It reuses the answer only for a matching client network; otherwise it performs another lookup.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
ECS makes part of the originating client's address visible to nameservers involved in the lookup and to networks carrying the DNS packets. The RFC recommends truncating IPv4 addresses to 24 bits and IPv6 addresses to 56 bits, while allowing users to request a zero-length source prefix when supported. It also recommends sending ECS only where it is useful and not to root, top-level, or public-suffix servers.

Forged ECS data can trigger extra queries, pollute caches, or increase cache pressure. Resolvers must check that the response's family, source prefix length, and address match the query. The RFC recommends limiting the number of networks and answers held in cache and treating ECS as a hint that an authoritative server may ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a shortened address reveals information about a client's network, so the RFC recommends limiting what is sent. Resolvers also need to check replies and limit cached network entries to reduce spoofing and resource risks.
